stem: Which nutrient is the central atom of the chlorophyll molecule?

options.content: Magnesium
options.rationale: Correct: each chlorophyll molecule has a magnesium atom at its centre.

options.content: Calcium, which is built into the walls of every leaf cell
options.rationale: Calcium is part of cell walls, not chlorophyll.

options.content: Potassium
options.rationale: Potassium controls stomata and activates enzymes; it is not part of chlorophyll.

options.content: Phosphorus
options.rationale: Phosphorus is needed for energy transfer (ATP) and roots.

explanation: Magnesium sits at the centre of chlorophyll, which is why a shortage causes chlorosis between the veins.

stem: Young maize seedlings in a cold, wet spell show a purple colour on their leaves. Which nutrient are they most likely short of?

options.content: Phosphorus
options.rationale: Correct: purpling is the classic sign of phosphorus deficiency in young maize.

options.content: Nitrogen, which is needed for proteins and chlorophyll
options.rationale: Nitrogen shortage gives pale yellow leaves, not purple.

options.content: Potassium
options.rationale: Potassium shortage scorches leaf margins.

options.content: Magnesium
options.rationale: Magnesium shortage gives yellow stripes between the veins.

explanation: Phosphorus deficiency shows as purple or reddish leaves; cold, wet soils slow phosphorus uptake by young roots.

stem: Which deficiency sign is typical of potassium shortage?

options.content: Purple leaves on young seedlings
options.rationale: That points to phosphorus.

options.content: Browning and scorching of the edges of older leaves
options.rationale: Correct: marginal scorch on older leaves is the typical sign.

options.content: A yellow V from the leaf tip down the midrib of lower leaves
options.rationale: That is the typical nitrogen sign in maize.

options.content: White bands on either side of the midrib of young leaves
options.rationale: That is zinc deficiency in maize.

explanation: Potassium is mobile, so it is moved out of old leaves, whose edges then scorch; stalks are also weak.

stem: Tomatoes on a farm near Mutare develop dark, sunken patches at the end of the fruit away from the stalk. Which nutrient problem is this?

options.content: Nitrogen excess
options.rationale: Too much nitrogen gives lush leaves, not this fruit disorder.

options.content: Sulfur deficiency
options.rationale: Sulfur shortage gives general yellowing of young leaves.

options.content: Calcium deficiency (blossom-end rot)
options.rationale: Correct: blossom-end rot is linked to too little calcium reaching the fruit.

options.content: Molybdenum deficiency, which causes whiptail in cauliflowers
options.rationale: Molybdenum is linked to whiptail in brassicas, not this tomato disorder.

explanation: Calcium is immobile and needed for cell walls; fruit tissue short of it collapses at the blossom end, often when watering is irregular.

stem: On a crop, the **youngest** leaves turn yellow between green veins while the older leaves stay green. Which nutrient is most likely lacking?

options.content: Magnesium
options.rationale: Magnesium causes interveinal chlorosis on older leaves, because it is mobile.

options.content: Nitrogen
options.rationale: Nitrogen yellowing starts on older leaves and is not limited to the spaces between veins.

options.content: Iron
options.rationale: Correct: iron is immobile, so its interveinal chlorosis appears on young leaves.

options.content: Potassium, which is moved to new growth when supply is short
options.rationale: Potassium is mobile, so it affects older leaves.

explanation: Interveinal chlorosis on young leaves points to an immobile nutrient such as iron; on old leaves the same pattern suggests magnesium.
hints: Is the nutrient mobile or immobile in the plant?
Mobile nutrients show first on old leaves.

stem: Groundnuts on a sandy soil produce many empty pods ("pops"). Which treatment would most directly correct this?

options.content: Extra ammonium nitrate as a top dressing at pegging
options.rationale: Groundnuts fix their own nitrogen; nitrogen does not fill pods.

options.content: Gypsum applied to the pegging zone at flowering
options.rationale: Correct: gypsum supplies calcium where the pods form.

options.content: Muriate of potash broadcast before planting
options.rationale: Extra potassium can even reduce calcium uptake.

options.content: A foliar spray of urea
options.rationale: Nitrogen is not the cause of empty pods.

explanation: Developing pods absorb calcium directly from the soil around them, so gypsum (calcium sulfate) is applied to the pegging zone at flowering.
hints: Which nutrient do developing groundnut pods take directly from the soil?

stem: A farmer applies twice the recommended nitrogen to a wheat crop. Which outcome is most likely?

options.content: Stronger stems, because nitrogen builds thicker cell walls
options.rationale: Calcium and potassium strengthen stems; extra nitrogen weakens them.

options.content: Earlier maturity and a higher grain yield in proportion to the extra nitrogen
options.rationale: Excess nitrogen delays maturity and yield does not rise in proportion.

options.content: Purple leaves, because nitrogen blocks phosphorus uptake
options.rationale: Purpling is a phosphorus sign; excess nitrogen gives dark green leaves.

options.content: Lush, soft growth that lodges and suffers more aphid and fungal attack
options.rationale: Correct: excess nitrogen weakens stems and attracts pests and diseases.

explanation: Too much nitrogen gives tall, soft plants with weak stems that fall over (lodge) and are more attractive to aphids and fungi; maturity is delayed and money is wasted.
hints: Think about what nitrogen does to leafy growth, and what happens when there is too much.

stem: Why is a shortage of molybdenum often seen first in legumes such as soya beans?

options.content: Legumes need molybdenum to make their seed coats hard
options.rationale: This is not the role of molybdenum.

options.content: Molybdenum is the main part of legume chlorophyll
options.rationale: Magnesium is in chlorophyll.

options.content: Legume roots release acids that destroy molybdenum in the soil
options.rationale: This is not why legumes are affected.

options.content: Molybdenum is needed for nitrogen fixation in the root nodules
options.rationale: Correct: without it the nodules fix little nitrogen and the plant yellows.

explanation: The nitrogen-fixing enzyme in *Rhizobium* nodules needs molybdenum, so molybdenum-deficient legumes show nitrogen-deficiency symptoms.
hints: What do legumes do that other crops do not?

stem: Trace elements are called minor nutrients because they are less important to the plant than nitrogen.
explanation: False. "Minor" refers only to the small amount needed; without a trace element the plant cannot grow normally.

stem: Deficiency of a mobile nutrient such as nitrogen shows first on the older, lower leaves of a plant.
explanation: True. The plant moves mobile nutrients from old leaves to new growth, so old leaves show the shortage first.

stem: Match each nutrient with its main function in the plant.

right.content: Opening and closing of stomata; strong stems
Formation of cell walls and growing points
Part of some amino acids and proteins
Part of proteins and chlorophyll; leafy growth
Energy transfer, root growth and seed formation

explanation: N proteins and chlorophyll; P energy, roots, seed; K stomata, enzymes and strength; Ca cell walls; S amino acids.

stem: Match each deficiency sign with the nutrient most likely to be lacking.

left.content: Yellow stripes between the veins of older maize leaves
White bands beside the midrib of young maize leaves
Hollow stems in cabbages and death of growing points

explanation: Interveinal striping of old maize leaves is magnesium; white bud is zinc; whiptail is molybdenum; hollow stem is boron.
hints: Two of these are trace elements of brassicas.

stem: Complete the sentences.

payload.template: Nutrients needed in large amounts are called {{blank:a}} nutrients. Yellowing of leaves caused by too little chlorophyll is called {{blank:b}}.

explanation: Major (macro) nutrients; chlorosis.

stem: In a sand-culture trial, bean seedlings in a complete solution had a mean dry mass of 18.0 g, and those in a solution with no magnesium 12.6 g. Calculate the percentage reduction in dry mass caused by leaving out magnesium.
explanation: Reduction = (18.0 − 12.6) ÷ 18.0 × 100 = 30%. Dividing 12.6 by 18.0 gives the mass remaining (70%), not the reduction.
workedSolution: 1. Reduction = (18.0 − 12.6) ÷ 18.0 × 100 = 30%. Dividing 12.6 by 18.0 gives the mass remaining (70%), not the reduction.

stem: Assume each tonne of sorghum grain removes 16 kg of nitrogen from the soil and ammonium nitrate contains 34.5% N. A farmer harvests 4.5 t/ha. Calculate the mass of ammonium nitrate needed to replace the nitrogen removed, in kg/ha, to one decimal place.
explanation: Nitrogen removed = 4.5 × 16 = 72 kg N/ha. Ammonium nitrate = 72 ÷ 0.345 = 208.7 kg/ha. Multiplying by 0.345 instead of dividing gives 24.8 kg, far too little.
workedSolution:
1. Nitrogen removed = 4.5 × 16 = 72 kg N/ha.
2. Each kg of ammonium nitrate contains 0.345 kg N.
3. Ammonium nitrate needed = 72 ÷ 0.345 = 208.7 kg/ha.
hints: Then divide by the fraction of N in the fertiliser.

stem: Name the nutrient whose deficiency causes empty pods ("pops") in groundnuts.
explanation: **Calcium**, supplied as gypsum at flowering.

stem: Explain why magnesium deficiency shows on the older leaves of a plant while calcium deficiency shows on the young leaves.

points.description: Magnesium is mobile: when supply is short the plant moves it from old leaves to new growth.
So the old leaves lose magnesium (chlorophyll) and show chlorosis first.
Calcium is immobile (fixed in cell walls), so new leaves and growing points cannot get it from old leaves and show the deficiency.

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: Magnesium is mobile in the plant, so when the soil supply runs short the plant moves magnesium out of the older leaves to the young growth; the older leaves then lose chlorophyll and turn yellow between the veins. Calcium is built into cell walls and cannot be moved again, so new leaves and growing points depend on fresh supply from the roots and are the first to be damaged.

explanation: The mobility of a nutrient decides where its deficiency appears.
hints: Which nutrient can the plant move from old to new leaves?

stem: Describe **two** harmful effects of applying too much nitrogen fertiliser to a crop and explain each.

points.description: Lush, soft growth / weak stems.
So the crop lodges and is attacked more by aphids and fungal diseases (or matures late).
Nitrate not used by the crop is leached.
So it pollutes groundwater and rivers (algal growth) and the money spent is wasted.

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: Too much nitrogen makes the crop grow lush and soft with weak stems, so it falls over (lodges) and is attacked more by aphids and fungi, lowering yield. The nitrate the crop cannot use is washed down by rain, so it pollutes groundwater and rivers, encouraging algae, and the farmer's money is wasted.

explanation: Give the effect and then its consequence.
hints: Think of the plant, and of the environment.

stem:
Form 1 pupils at a school near Gweru grew maize seedlings in culture solutions. All pots had the same light, temperature and volume of solution.

| Culture solution | Mean dry mass (g) | Appearance after four weeks |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Complete | 32.0 | Dark green, upright |
| No nitrogen | 11.2 | Pale yellow, older leaves first |
| No phosphorus | 17.6 | Purple tinge on leaves, small roots |
| No calcium | 20.8 | Tips of young leaves hooked and dead |

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem: Calculate the percentage reduction in dry mass caused by leaving out nitrogen.

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: Why was a pot with the complete solution included?

options.content: To supply extra nutrients that could flow into the other pots
options.rationale: Each pot is separate.

options.content: To prove that maize needs no phosphorus at all
options.rationale: The no-phosphorus pots grew less, so phosphorus is needed.

options.content: As a control, to compare the effect of each missing nutrient
options.rationale: Correct: it shows normal growth for comparison.

options.content: To make the whole experiment take less time to complete
options.rationale: The control does not shorten the trial.

parts.explanation: The complete solution is the control: any difference in the other pots is due to the missing nutrient.

parts.label: (c)
parts.stem: Name the nutrient that is immobile in the plant, as shown by where its symptoms appeared.
parts.explanation: Calcium: symptoms on the young leaf tips show it cannot be moved from old leaves.

parts.label: (d)
parts.stem: Explain why the plants with no nitrogen were pale yellow.

points.description: Nitrogen is part of chlorophyll (and proteins).
Without it little chlorophyll is made, so leaves yellow (chlorosis), starting with older leaves as nitrogen is moved to new growth.

parts.label: (e)
parts.stem: Suggest **two** ways of improving this experiment.

points.description: Use more pots (replicates) for each solution and take the mean.
Include more solutions (e.g. no potassium, no magnesium) / grow for longer / measure root mass and height too / use seeds of one variety and equal size.

explanation: Calculate from the table, then explain the symptoms using the function and mobility of each nutrient.
hints: Use the position of the symptoms (old or young leaves).

stem: Chipo grows tomatoes and cabbages in a school garden near Chinhoyi. The tomatoes have weak growth with brown, scorched leaf edges on the older leaves and small fruit. Some cabbages have hollow stems, and their growing points have died.

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem: Name the nutrient most likely lacking in the tomatoes.
parts.explanation: Marginal scorch of older leaves and small fruit point to potassium.

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: Name the trace element most likely lacking in the cabbages.
parts.explanation: Hollow stems and dead growing points in brassicas point to boron.

parts.label: (c)
parts.stem: State **two** functions of the nutrient you named in (a).

points.description: Controls opening and closing of stomata / water balance.
Activates enzymes / moves sugars / strengthens stems / disease resistance / fruit quality.

parts.label: (d)
parts.stem: Explain why trace elements must be applied with great care.

points.description: They are needed in very small amounts and the range between enough and too much is narrow.
An overdose is toxic and can scorch or kill the crop.

parts.explanation: Small requirement, high risk of toxicity.

explanation: Read the symptoms, name the nutrient, then explain its role and the risk of overuse.
hints: Use the position and type of each symptom.

stem: A farmer says: "If my maize is yellow, I only need to add more ammonium nitrate." Discuss this statement.

points.description: Nitrogen shortage is a common cause: yellowing of old leaves in a V along the midrib.
But magnesium deficiency gives interveinal striping of old leaves and needs magnesium (e.g. dolomitic lime), not nitrogen.
Sulfur, iron or zinc shortage give yellowing of young leaves.
Waterlogging, root damage, pests or diseases (e.g. maize streak virus) can also yellow leaves.
Extra nitrogen when it is not the cause wastes money and may cause lodging and leaching.
Judgement: diagnose first (position and pattern of symptoms, soil test) before adding fertiliser.

levels.descriptor: Accurate, well-developed explanation of several relevant points using correct agricultural terms, applied to the crop, animal or situation in the question, with a clear judgement where one is asked for.
Some relevant points explained, partly developed or only partly applied to the situation; any judgement is simple or one-sided.
Simple statements or a list of points with little explanation or application.

answerSpec.modelAnswer: The farmer may be right if the yellowing starts on the lower leaves as a V down the midrib, the typical sign of nitrogen shortage, especially after heavy rain on sandy soil. But other causes look similar. Magnesium shortage gives yellow stripes between the veins of old leaves; sulfur, iron and zinc shortages show on young leaves; waterlogging, root pests and diseases such as maize streak virus also yellow maize. Adding ammonium nitrate then wastes money, may cause soft growth and lodging, and the nitrate may be leached. The farmer should look at where and how the leaves are yellow and test the soil before deciding.

explanation: Weigh nitrogen against other causes and conclude that diagnosis comes first.
hints: Is nitrogen the only cause of yellow leaves?
Where on the plant is the yellowing?
